title: Bartholin Abscess & Vulvar Emergencies
keywords: expanding vulvar hematoma > 5 cm to OR

sources: Critical Vector — OB Pocket Guide: Bartholin Abscess & Vulvar Emergencies (ACOG 2022)
ACOG / StatPearls on Bartholin gland cyst and abscess; obstetric laceration repair

changelog.change: Initial entry — Bartholin abscess (Word catheter vs marsupialisation, biopsy indication), postpartum vulvar haematoma, and layered laceration repair including the fourth-degree sequence.

summary: Drain a Bartholin abscess AND place a Word catheter — simple incision and drainage alone recurs. Send the cyst wall for pathology in any patient ≥ 40 (Bartholin gland carcinoma). An expanding postpartum vulvar haematoma goes to the operating room.

items: Unilateral, tender, fluctuant labial swelling at the 4 or 8 o'clock position of the introitus; a non-tender swelling without inflammation is a cyst, not an abscess.
Fever or spreading erythema suggests cellulitis or an abscess extending beyond the gland.

rows: Stab incision on the mucosal (inner) surface; drain; insert the catheter and inflate the balloon with 2–3 mL saline. Leave 4–6 weeks for a re-epithelialised tract
Sew the cyst-wall edges to the skin edges to create a permanent opening — preferred for recurrent abscesses
High recurrence — only if a Word catheter is unavailable
Not needed for an uncomplicated drained abscess. Add for cellulitis, immunocompromise, pregnancy, or SSTI risk; cover gonorrhoea/chlamydia + anaerobes if an STI is likely
Age ≥ 40 — send the cyst wall for histology (Bartholin gland carcinoma risk)

items: A rapidly expanding, exquisitely painful perineal or vulvar mass after delivery.
Infralevator (vulvar) — most common; supralevator — extends into the broad ligament, harder to detect, larger blood loss.
Small (< 5 cm), stable: ice, analgesia, close observation.
Expanding, or > 5 cm: operating room for evacuation, haemostasis (figure-of-eight sutures), and a drain. Interventional radiology for a supralevator haematoma or ongoing arterial bleeding.
Resuscitate and transfuse to the clinical picture — the visible haematoma underestimates the loss.
Identify the APEX of the laceration before starting — it may require examination under anaesthesia; a suture placed below the true apex leaves a bleeding vessel.
Repair in layers with a delayed-absorbable suture; ensure haemostasis.

Fourth-degree sequence: rectal mucosa (fine absorbable, submucosal) → internal anal sphincter → external anal sphincter (end-to-end or overlapping) → anal-sphincter-complex fascia → vaginal mucosa → perineal muscle → perineal skin.

Perform a rectal exam after the repair to confirm no suture has passed through the rectal mucosa. Single-dose antibiotics (e.g. a second-generation cephalosporin) reduce wound complications after a third/fourth-degree tear.
